item.title: Harvesters query rate cut
item.description: MECHANICAL harvesting operators will need to seek clarification from the Fiji Competition and Consumer Commission (FCCC) over the recent review of harvesting rates, says Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna. Mr Tunabuna was responding to concerns from operators after FCCC revised the mechanical harvesting rate from $24.63 a tonne to $20.52 a tonne following a decline in fuel prices.
item.content:encoded:
MECHANICAL harvesting operators will need to seek clarification from the Fiji Competition and Consumer Commission (FCCC) over the recent review of harvesting rates, says Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna.

Mr Tunabuna was responding to concerns from operators after FCCC revised the mechanical harvesting rate from $24.63 a tonne to $20.52 a tonne following a decline in fuel prices.

The revised rate represents a 16.7 per cent reduction from the previous interim rate.

Some operators have raised concerns that the reduction could affect their ability to provide harvesting services.

Mr Tunabuna said FCCC was responsible for explaining the basis of the review and how the revised rates were calculated.

“I’m not sure how they formulate their formula charges. They will have to explain.”

He said adjustments to harvesting rates were part of the normal review process and were linked to changes in fuel costs.

“The fuel subsidy that was given to them will be readjusted when there is a change in fuel. That’s very normal practice.”

Mr Tunabuna said stakeholders should engage with FCCC over the revised rates, as mechanical harvesting operators remained an important part of the sugar industry.

item.title: Sugar sector row pits Chaudhry, Prof Biman
item.description: FORMER prime minister and National Farmers Union general secretary Mahendra Chaudhry has criticised Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka over discussions to privatise the Fiji Sugar Corporation, accusing him of making statements without taking action. Mr Chaudhry questioned Mr Rabuka’s understanding of the sugar sector following comments about a possible sale of the State-owned sugar miller to a private
item.content:encoded:
FORMER prime minister and National Farmers Union general secretary Mahendra Chaudhry has criticised Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka over discussions to privatise the Fiji Sugar Corporation, accusing him of making statements without taking action.

Mr Chaudhry questioned Mr Rabuka’s understanding of the sugar sector following comments about a possible sale of the State-owned sugar miller to a private entity.

He claimed that despite establishing a Special Parliamentary Committee on Sugar in July last year to address long-standing industry challenges, the Prime Minister had not convened a meeting of the body.

“He hasn’t called a single meeting of that committee since it was formed,” Mr Chaudhry said. “If he says he is trying to privatise the industry to sell it to somebody, I don’t think he understands the situation properly.”

Mr Chaudhry accused the Prime Minister of ignoring cane growers while challenges in the industry continued.

However, National Federation Party leader and Parliamentary Sugar Select Committee member Professor Biman Prasad rejected Mr Chaudhry’s criticism, saying he was responsible for the decline of sugar industry institutions.

“He is the man who was responsible for the destruction of the sugar industry institutions,” Prof Prasad said.

He defended the committee’s work, saying members, chaired by the Prime Minister, had conducted field visits across Viti Levu to meet growers, with visits to Vanua Levu planned.

He said the committee was assessing both immediate relief measures and long-term strategies for the industry.

Prof Prasad said sugarcane farmers under the current administration had received the highest cane prices in the country’s history, with further recommendations being considered to address challenges, including the impact of the fuel crisis.

Questions sent to Mr Rabuka remained unanswered when this edition went to press last night.

item.title: Tunabuna hits out at NFU’s absence
item.description: NATIONAL Farmers Union (NFU) general secretary Mahendra Chaudhry has been vocal on social media about issues affecting the sugar industry but did not attend consultations with farmers and stakeholders, says Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna. Mr Tunabuna made the comments in response to Mr Chaudhry’s recent statement calling on the Government to address concerns raised by cane farmers and challenges f
item.content:encoded:
NATIONAL Farmers Union (NFU) general secretary Mahendra Chaudhry has been vocal on social media about issues affecting the sugar industry but did not attend consultations with farmers and stakeholders, says Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna.

Mr Tunabuna made the comments in response to Mr Chaudhry’s recent statement calling on the Government to address concerns raised by cane farmers and challenges facing the sugar industry.

Mr Chaudhry had criticised the Government’s response to harvesting difficulties and said concerns over cane prices and payments needed to be addressed to improve cane supply.

However, Mr Tunabuna said he was disappointed Mr Chaudhry did not participate in discussions despite claiming to represent farmers.

“He can be very vocal on social media, but he hasn’t really been coming forward,” Mr Tunabuna said.

He said Mr Chaudhry had written to Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka and copied him on a letter outlining several demands before the crushing season.

“He clearly mentioned that they were not boycotting, but they had their demands, and they were going to harvest. Their demands were met.”

Mr Tunabuna said he had attempted to arrange a meeting with Mr Chaudhry to discuss the issues raised.

He said consultations were later held with farmers and transport service providers in various areas, involving the Prime Minister, Opposition Leader, senior Government officials and Members of Parliament.

“Although he said he was representing farmers, he was not in any of those forums.”

Mr Tunabuna said it was disappointing that concerns were being raised publicly when opportunities were available for direct discussions with stakeholders.

item.title: ‘FSC needs new mills’
item.description: Rakiraki businessman and cane grower George Shiu Raj has backed the proposal to privatise the Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC), but says the country’s ageing sugar mills must first be replaced. His comments follow Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s suggestion in Cakaudrove this week that the Government was considering privatising FSC.
item.content:encoded:
Rakiraki businessman and cane grower George Shiu Raj has backed the proposal to privatise the Fiji Sugar Corporation (FSC), but says the country’s ageing sugar mills must first be replaced.

His comments follow Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s suggestion in Cakaudrove this week that the Government was considering privatising FSC.

“Now, the honourable Prime Minister is saying to sell the sugar mills to the private sector,” Mr Shiu Raj said.

“It’s a good idea, not a bad one, but probably we have to ask who is going to buy it? These two mills (Lautoka and Rarawai) are very old mills now.

“They were built during the British Colonial Sugar Refining Company era, and we have to look into how we can operate these mills.”

Mr Shiu Raj said the Chinese government had offered to assist the current administration with building a new mill in 2025. He said the proposed mill would process 1.9 million tonnes of cane, with the Chinese company requiring land capable of producing 300,000 tonnes of cane and buying the remaining 1.6 million tonnes from farmers.

“That is a good idea if a new mill can be built because the two mills in Lautoka and Ba are very old mills and this is why FSC is not making money,” he said.

Mr Shiu Raj said operating costs were high whenever the ageing mills experienced breakdowns.

“The mills are very old, and the honourable Prime Minister likes to say that we can now probably sell these mills to the private sector.

“But we have to produce more cane, not 1.5 million tonnes of cane from the Northern and Western divisions.

“It would be a good idea if the farmers can get four million tonnes of cane.”

He said the sugar industry needed a new mill to ensure its long-term sustainability.

Mr Shiu Raj said a new mill in the Western Division capable of processing between 1.9 million and 2.5 million tonnes of cane would help increase production, reduce costs and improve profitability.

“FSC would have more than 2.2 million tonnes of cane to have a profit.

“We got only 1.4 million tonne or 1.5 million tonne; that is why FSC is not making money.”

In November last year, a delegation from the People’s Republic of China presented a proposal for a new sugar mill project to former Sugar Minister Charan Jeath Singh, Member of Parliament Professor Biman Prasad, FSC board chair Nitya Reddy, board members and former permanent secretary Dr Vinesh Kumar at the FSC Training Centre in Lautoka.

The China National Machinery Import and Export Corporation team outlined initial mill designs, proposed technology upgrades and a possible funding model.

The Government had committed to building a new mill in the Western Division but has not disclosed its location.

item.description: A centuries-old tradition on the chiefly island of Bau made way for a rare exception yesterday as the Ulu ni Vuaka, the sacred meeting house of chiefs was transformed into a formal dining hall with tables and chairs for the vakataraisulu ceremony honouring the late Turaga na Taukei Naisogolaca Ratu Epeli Nailatikau. item.content:encoded:
A centuries-old tradition on the chiefly island of Bau made way for a rare exception yesterday as the Ulu ni Vuaka, the sacred meeting house of chiefs was transformed into a formal dining hall with tables and chairs for the vakataraisulu ceremony honouring the late Turaga na Taukei Naisogolaca Ratu Epeli Nailatikau.

The historic gesture welcomed chiefly guests from Lau and Bau during one of the ceremony’s most significant gatherings.

Traditionally, meetings held in the Ulu ni Vuaka required everyone to sit on mats spread across the floor, with the high chiefs occupying the head of the gathering.

However, yesterday, the Ulu ni Vuaka took on a different appearance after the women of Nasogolaca successfully sought permission to arrange tables and chairs for distinguished guests.

Arieta Kabukivuya, who helped prepare the venue, said such approval was granted only on exceptional occasions.

“The last time tables and chairs were set up in the Ulu ni Vuaka was in 2023 when Bau hosted the Bose Levu Vakaturaga,” she said.

“Now because of such a memorable occasion such as the vakataraisulu, we have been granted the exception.”

She said the women began work early in the morning to ensure the house was ready before guests arrived for lunch.

“It was an honour for us to prepare the house.

“We wanted everything to reflect the respect and dignity of the occasion.”

item.title: Mourning period ends
item.description: THE solemn 100-night mourning period for the late Turaga na Taukei Nasogolaca, Ratu Epeli Nailatikau, came to an end yesterday as members of the chiefly household and the vanua of Lau gathered to observe the sacred vakataraisulu ceremony, a significant custom that marks the lifting of mourning. item.content:encoded:
THE solemn 100-night mourning period for the late Turaga na Taukei Nasogolaca, Ratu Epeli Nailatikau, came to an end yesterday as members of the chiefly household and the vanua of Lau gathered to observe the sacred vakataraisulu ceremony, a significant custom that marks the lifting of mourning.

At the heart of the ceremony was the widow of the late statesman, Adi Koila Nailatikau, who removed the black mourning attire she had worn over the past 100 nights, symbolising the conclusion of her period of mourning and the family’s transition into the next chapter following Ratu Epeli’s passing.

In accordance with customs, Ratu Epeli’s daughter, Adi Litia Nailatikau, was dressed in layers of traditional mats, cloth and masi, signifying the honour bestowed upon the chiefly household during the vakataraisulu.

She was then escorted to Matawelagi, the residence of the Turaga Vunivalu na Tui Kaba, where she took part in the sacred luva ni sulu ceremony, during which her ceremonial attire was formally removed.

While Adi Litia was being adorned, the vanua o Lau led by Tui Nayau Ratu Tevita Uluilakeba Mara made its way to Nasogolaca, the residence of the late Ratu Epeli, to present traditional offerings to the chiefly family before the commencement of the official proceedings, reaffirming the enduring bonds between the people of Lau and Bau.

Following the luva ni sulu ceremony at Matawelagi, the chiefly party proceeded to Naicobocobo, the residence of the Roko Tui Bau, where Adi Litia Mara Dugdale also participated in the traditional luva i sulu, continuing a custom that has been observed within the chiefly households of Bau for generations.

Speaking on behalf of the Tui Kaba clan, Apenisa Seniloli said the people of Bau had spent the week preparing for the important occasion, which unfolded over three days.

“We had been preparing since Monday for this significant ceremony,” he said.

As part of the traditional observances, the women of Bau gathered on Thursday for the duki, which marked the lifting of the qoliqoli tabu, ending the prohibition that had been placed on the island’s traditional fishing grounds during the mourning period.

The vakataraisulu is among the most significant mourning customs of Bau, symbolising not only the conclusion of the 100 nights of mourning but also the restoration of the chiefly household and the wider vanua to everyday life after a period of reverence and remembrance. The late Ratu Epeli, Fiji’s former president and a chief of Bau, was accorded a State funeral on April 17 before he was laid to rest at the chiefly burial ground on Bau Island.

item.title: Rabuka stands by MSG appointment
item.description: THE appointment of Dr Anna Naupa as the new Melanesian Spearhead Group (MSG) director-general was made through an independent selection process. These were the words of Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka who said she was the best applicant.
item.content:encoded:
THE appointment of Dr Anna Naupa as the new Melanesian Spearhead Group (MSG) director-general was made through an independent selection process.

These were the words of Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka who said she was the best applicant.

Mr Rabuka made the comments in response to criticism from Vanuatu chiefs who said the regional position should have been held by a man rather than a woman.

He told this newspaper the recruitment process was merit-based.

“She came out as the preferred candidate. In fact, she came out top of the list,” he said.

Asked whether the comments from Vanuatu could create instability within the MSG, Mr Rabuka declined to comment on the country’s position.

“I will not speak on what Vanuatu has said and their views on that particular issue. But in general, we pick the best candidate, and we’re still going with our gender-positive policies.

“We have to be considerate. I know culturally the Melanesians are new to the culture of gender equality, but it’s something that we have to grasp and go with.”

Dr Naupa became the first woman to be appointed director-general of the MSG Secretariat following a regional recruitment process involving all MSG member countries.

item.title: Kula Awards return
item.description: The Kula Awards, Film Fiji’s national secondary schools creative arts competition, will return this year after a seven-year break, offering students a platform to showcase their talents and gain industry experience. Film Fiji chief executive Jone Robertson said the awards were suspended because of COVID-19 after running for 14 years.
item.content:encoded:
The Kula Awards, Film Fiji’s national secondary schools creative arts competition, will return this year after a seven-year break, offering students a platform to showcase their talents and gain industry experience.

Film Fiji chief executive Jone Robertson said the awards were suspended because of COVID-19 after running for 14 years.

“There is not really a creative arts or performing arts platform where kids can showcase their talent and their skills,” he said.

The program includes filmmaking and dance workshops, with students receiving hands-on training from industry professionals.

Film students recently visited the set of US Survivor on Mana Island, where the production crew conducted camera and filmmaking workshops. Dance participants are also being mentored by VOU.

Mr Robertson said the initiative aimed to inspire young people to pursue careers in the creative sector and provide positive pathways for their future.
